prompt: A team has a polished Jenkins pipeline that runs on every push. Developers work on feature branches for three to four weeks before merging to `main`. Are they practising continuous integration?

options.text: No; CI means integrating into the mainline at least daily, with each integration verified automatically
options.explanation: Correct. They have automated builds, but not continuous *integration*. Their integration happens in big, infrequent merges.

options.text: Yes, as long as the builds are green
options.explanation: Green builds on isolated branches say nothing about whether the branches work together. The integration itself is delayed by weeks.

options.text: Yes; they have a CI server running automated builds
options.explanation: This confuses the tool with the practice. Continuous integration means integrating into the mainline frequently, and four-week branches are the opposite.

options.text: No, because Jenkins is not a CI tool
options.explanation: Jenkins is one of the oldest and most widely used CI servers. The problem is the branching practice, not the tool.

workedExample:
Check the two halves of Fowler's definition:

1. Does everyone integrate into the mainline frequently (at least daily)? No: every 3-4 weeks.
2. Is each integration verified by an automated build and tests? The branches are, but the real integration (the merge) happens rarely.

So they get automated testing benefits, but not CI's main benefit: discovering conflicts and semantic clashes within hours.

prompt: Your pipeline runs: end-to-end tests (18 min), then unit tests (3 min), then lint (40 s). Lint failures are the most frequent cause of red builds. What is the most effective reordering?

options.text: Remove lint from CI and rely on developers to run it
options.explanation: Lint failing often shows developers aren't running it reliably. CI is the backstop; pre-commit hooks can help too.

options.text: Keep the order; end-to-end tests are most important so they should run first
options.explanation: Importance doesn't decide order; feedback time does. Running the slowest step first delays every common failure.

options.text: Unit tests, then end-to-end, then lint
options.explanation: Lint, the most common failure and the cheapest check, would still be reported last, after about 21 minutes.

options.text: Lint, then unit tests, then end-to-end tests
options.explanation: Correct. Fail fast: the cheapest and most frequently failing checks go first, so lint failures are reported within a minute rather than after 21 minutes.

workedExample:
Time to discover a lint failure:

| Order | Lint result after |
|---|---|
| E2E, unit, lint | About 21.7 min |
| Lint, unit, E2E | 0.7 min |

And unit failures move from about 21 to about 3.7 minutes. Better still, run lint and unit tests in parallel jobs, then make E2E wait for both.
